description.value: The study investigated brain activation, heart rate variability, and their coupling during paced breathing, psychosocial stress induction, and stress recovery.

design.value: Thirty-two healthy right-handed adults underwent a single MRI-scanning session while completing unpaced breathing, normal-paced breathing, deep-paced breathing, the Montreal Imaging Stress Task, and recovery deep-paced breathing. The study combined block-design fMRI with continuous photoplethysmography-derived heart-rate measures and respiration monitoring.

description.value: 35 healthy participants were recruited through community advertisements; three participants were excluded due to excessive head movement, leading to a sample size of N = 32.

inclusion_criteria.value: no neurological disorder or head injury

exclusion_criteria.value: excessive head movement during scanning (> 4 mm, ± 3° of rotation)

medical_condition.value: healthy; no mental illness history, neurological disorder, or head injury

task_description.value: The task consisted of 4 min of unpaced breathing, 4 min of normal-paced breathing at 10 breaths/min, 4 min of deep-paced breathing at 5.5 breaths/min, the Montreal Imaging Stress Task, and a 4-min recovery-from-stress block of deep breathing at 5.5 breaths/min.

presentation_software.value: Presentation V18 (Neurobehavioral Systems, Berkeley, Calif., USA)

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to follow a paced breathing exercise and to solve simple arithmetic tasks and submit their response via a response button box.

stimuli.value: Visual breathing cues, simple arithmetic problems, and feedback indicating whether responses were correct, incorrect, or too slow, together with a mock performance bar.

task_performance_measures.value: Responses to simple arithmetic tasks submitted via a response button box

instrument.value: Prisma Fit 3-T whole-body MR scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a standard 32-channel head coil

description.value: 40 oblique interleaved slices were acquired parallel to the AC-PC axis using a T2*-sensitive single-shot EPI sequence. A total of 500 images were collected during one single run.

instrument.value: Prisma Fit 3-T whole-body MR scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany)

description.value: High-resolution T1 MPRAGE anatomical images were acquired for anatomical reference.

instrument.value: PPG sensor attached to the proximal phalanx of the left index finger; built-in system provided by the MRI vendor

description.value: Heart rate was continuously monitored during scanning. Local maxima of the PPG signal were automatically detected and timestamps of PPG peaks were recorded by the MR scanner.

reason_no_modality_class_used.value: The recording is a physiological PPG signal rather than MRI, EEG, fNIRS, or PET.

instrument.value: Inductive plethysmography via a respiratory cushion integrated into a belt, connected by a pressure hose to the ECG and respiratory sensor unit (PERU)

description.value: Respiration was continuously measured using inductive plethysmography; the PERU recorded respiration curves in real time. The respiratory signal was acquired using a built-in system provided by the MRI vendor.

reason_no_modality_class_used.value: The recording is a respiratory physiological signal rather than MRI, EEG, fNIRS, or PET.

description.value: fMRI preprocessing was conducted using SPM12 and included removal of the first four volumes, slice time correction, realignment and unwarping, coregistration, normalization to MNI space, and smoothing.

steps.value: Exclusion of first four volumes to account for magnetic field equilibration
Realignment and unwarping to correct for artifacts due to susceptibility-by-movement interactions
Coregistration of T1 images with the mean T2* images
Normalization to MNI space (functional: 3 mm3, anatomical: 1 mm3)
Smoothing of functional images using an 8 mm Gaussian kernel

description.value: PPG peak detection was manually inspected; errors due to ectopic beats or participant movement were identified using a 30% interval-change filter and interpolated. IBI and RMSSD time series were resampled at the fMRI TR and mean-centered for sliding-window analyses.

steps.value: Manual inspection of peak detection by overlapping scanner-detected peak timestamps over the PPG signal
Identification of errors in peaks due to ectopic beats or participant movement using a percentage filter
Resampling of IBI and RMSSD time series at the fMRI TR

model_settings.value: Block design; different events were modeled using boxcar functions; a 480 s high-pass filter was used. Individual contrasts were constructed for Relaxation, Stress Reactivity, Stress Recovery Specific Relaxation, Post Stress Relaxation, and additional baseline comparisons.
Natural log-corrected IBI and RMSSD values were compared across task blocks; post hoc comparisons used Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference test.

estimator.value: Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference test for post hoc comparisons

model_settings.value: Brain activation time series from seven a priori defined ROIs were modeled as smooth terms predicting RMSSD or IBI. Experimental condition, subjects, and time points were included as parametric terms. Thin plate regression splines were used; smoothing parameters were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

model_type.value: Granger causality analysis using vector autoregressive (VAR) models

model_settings.value: For each HRV–ROI pair, bivariate VAR models were fitted. The optimal lag order was determined using the Akaike Information Criterion. Statistical significance was evaluated using 1,000 permutations generated by independently shuffling HRV and ROI time series across time points, with Bonferroni correction.

estimator.value: Akaike Information Criterion for lag selection and permutation-based null distribution for significance testing

description.value: 4 min of normal breathing in which participants were free to breathe at their own pace.
4 min of breathing at a normal rate of 10 breaths/min; this block served as the control condition for deep-paced breathing.
4 min of slow breathing at a frequency of 5.5 breaths/min.

Modified Montreal Imaging Stress Task combining high cognitive demand with negative social evaluation; participants solved arithmetic problems under individually calculated time limits and received manipulated performance feedback.
4-min recovery-from-stress block of deep breathing at 5.5 breaths/min.
